heading: Farming for market and community
body: Your garden gives food, income and useful knowledge.
This section shows how to keep records, sell surplus harvest and build a local food network.
The aim is a farm that feeds the household and works like a small, clear economy.

heading: Why this matters
body: A harvest can feed the household, be sold, be shared, or be lost.
Recording these different uses helps you see what the farm produces and what reaches customers.
Use that information to protect household food and make better business decisions.

heading: Learning outcomes
body: At the end, you will be able to record harvests and where they go.
You will be able to count the real costs of production before setting the price.
You will be able to connect surplus harvest with a suitable customer or way of selling.
You will be able to build a local network of seed, tools, skills and food.

heading: Watch: what a farm record shows
body: The record follows each harvest to household food, to sales, to gifts or to compost.
Read through the whole year to see the farm as an economy before making a business decision.

heading: Record every harvest
body: Write down every harvest as it happens.
Record kg of tomatoes, dozens of eggs and bunches of vegetables (morogo), and note where each went.
Use the same simple habit for food kept at home, produce sold, that given to others and that made into compost.
Do not rely on memory at the end of the season.

heading: Let one season answer questions
body: Records of one season answer practical questions.
Which crops give a better harvest in each bed? Which return the most per hour of work?
Which crops use more seed, water and compost than they return?
The record also shows which months leave the household buying food.

heading: Find the real costs
body: Before setting a price, record production costs, packaging and selling costs, including labour and transport.
Here is a teaching example, not a market price: the cost of producing tomatoes is R18 per kilogram but they are sold at R15 per kilogram. This price does not cover the stated costs.
Review price, costs and the next planting. Check what customers will really buy; a high asking price is not a guarantee of sales.

heading: Plan the food gap
body: Use your record to find the time when household food runs out.
Choose crops that suit where you live, and work backwards from the harvest you need. Check planting conditions and expected harvest time.
A date that works on another farm may not work here. Include a back-up plan for if rain, water or crops fail.

heading: Watch: where the surplus harvest can go
body: Surplus harvest can leave the farm via a roadside stall, delivered by a group to a shop, or by a box delivered to a house.
The 'iintolo' (unknown word) show each route.

heading: Know your customer
body: Ask what the customer wants: product, quantity, quality, delivery and payment date.
Compare market fees, transport, packaging and unsold products together with the selling price.
Check market rules and local trade and food requirements. A stall that is not formal is not automatically one without rules or costs.

heading: Count the work of direct selling
body: Direct selling can keep a large part of the sale price, but it takes time, packaging, transport and looking after customers.
A box scheme provides a regular selection of produce regularly to customers who agree with you.
Agree on what goes in the box, price, payment and what happens when crops are scarce. Regular orders help planning only when customers and farmers can keep the agreement.

heading: Plan by real orders
body: Start from what you can supply reliably and what customers want.
Check costs and household food needs before promising regular boxes.
Garden size or number of customers alone does not tell you the income. Try an arrangement you can control and record the results.

heading: Match the way of selling to your supply
body: If produce changes week by week, avoid promising unchanging delivery that you cannot supply.
Offer the surplus harvest you have and agree clear terms with customers.
Describe your farming methods honestly. Check any certificate or standard that customers require before using the label.

heading: Watch: how neighbours strengthen the harvest
body: One farm can produce food.
A group can share seed, tools, skills and transport.
Different farmers become a strong local food network, each household contributing according to its ability.

heading: Save seed together
body: Neighbours can share varieties and the work of keeping seed.
Record crop, variety, source and date of collection. Plan proper separation (keeping crops apart), selection, drying and storage for each crop.
Sharing does not automatically increase diversity or improve quality. Confirm what the seed truly is and whether it germinates before relying on shared seed.
Before exchanging seed, check whether the variety is protected and whether permission is needed.

heading: Share expensive tools
body: Sharing tools makes expensive tools accessible to a group.
A water pump or grain mill may be out of reach of one household's budget.
Shared use spreads cost across the group and helps each farm do work it might not do alone.

heading: Reduce losses between harvest and sale
body: Handle harvest carefully and keep shade, packaging and proper storage until delivery is finished.
A nearby customer may reduce travel, but losses and selling costs still need to be balanced.
Compare money received after fees, transport and spoilage for each route. Do not assume the nearby customer is always the one giving the best profit.

heading: Share skills and check results
body: Neighbours can show useful skills and compare what happens on their farms.
Record method, conditions and result so others can judge whether it might suit their land.
Seek advice from trained people when there is an unusual disease or technical problems. Shared experience and the help of professionals can work together.

heading: Field task: make a farm record
body: Use headings: harvest, where it went, costs and work.
Record each kilogram, dozen or bunch as it leaves the farm.
Include food kept by the household, produce sold, that given to others and that made into compost.
At the end of a season, identify the crop that returns well together with the month in which the household buys food.

heading: Field action: use the record
body: Choose one real decision in your farm record.
Compare costs and profit of a crop or selling method, or plan the household food gap using local growing conditions.

Then agree with neighbours on one working activity: seed swap, tool sharing, joint delivery or skills session. Before exchanging seed, check whether the variety is protected and whether permission is needed. Record responsibility and review what happens.
